analysis.one_liner: Requires consent before TSA uses facial recognition at airport checkpoints and restricts storing or sharing the data.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to require consent before TSA scans travelers' faces has sat in the Senate Commerce Committee with no action since its May 2025 referral.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would limit how the Transportation Security Administration uses facial recognition at airport checkpoints. Travelers would have to be told and give affirmative consent before their face is scanned; anyone who opts out would be verified with a regular photo ID instead, with no penalty or extra screening. It would also bar TSA from sharing travelers' biometric data, set short deadlines for deleting it, prohibit using the technology for wide-scale tracking, and require annual government audits of the technology's accuracy and bias.
analysis.who_benefits: Every air traveler in the United States. Today, TSA can scan a passenger's face at the checkpoint with little in the way of notice or a genuine choice to decline. The bill would make facial scans strictly opt-in for regular passengers and opt-out for trusted-traveler members, require that opting out carry no penalty or extra screening, forbid sharing biometric data outside TSA, force deletion of previously collected images, and ban the technology from being used for wide-scale tracking (S2, S3). People who fly rarely, lack smartphones, or simply don't want their face in a government database gain the most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Air travelers facing TSA face scans

how_it_helps.text: Travelers would get a real choice: regular passengers would be verified with a standard photo ID by default, and TSA could only use facial recognition on them after clear notice and affirmative express consent before each use — standing in line or entering the checkpoint would not count as consent.

Passengers who decline the face scan could not be subjected to discriminatory treatment, extra screening, or less favorable conditions, and TSA would have to verify them with an approved ID document without collecting any biometric information.

The bill would stop TSA from sharing biometric data outside the agency, require facial images to be deleted shortly after identity verification (24 hours after scheduled departure for 1:N matching), and force disposal of previously collected images that would violate the new rules.

It would prohibit TSA from using facial recognition to track or identify passengers outside the screening checkpoint or to enable systemic, wide-scale surveillance, and would require annual, publicly released audits of the technology's effectiveness, false-match rates, and racial, ethnic, age, and sex bias.

analysis.who_pays: TSA would bear the cost of maintaining ID-document verification lanes, signage, announcements, and deletion systems for biometric data, and companies that sell facial recognition systems to TSA would lose a growing federal deployment. Travelers bear essentially no direct cost; the bill leaves standard ID checks — the traditional method — fully intact.

drawbacks.text: The bill is not a full ban: trusted-traveler (Global Entry, PreCheck) members could still be face-scanned at the checkpoint unless they affirmatively opt out, and TSA could keep test images for up to 90 days under a testing-and-evaluation exception.

It covers only TSA's use of the technology at screening. Airlines' own use of facial recognition for boarding and other airport uses are outside the bill's restrictions, so biometric collection in airports could continue through the private side.

TSA and security officials argue facial matching speeds up checkpoint identity checks; requiring a parallel ID-document process and new notification systems could add operating cost and some friction, which the bill addresses only by requiring annual audits of the technology's effect on cost and passenger experience rather than resolving it directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The privacy protections are substantial and the cost is modest: identity verification would still happen for every passenger, just with a photo ID rather than a face scan unless the passenger consents. The main honest criticisms are that trusted travelers still face an opt-out (rather than opt-in) system, images can be retained up to 90 days for testing, and the bill leaves airlines' facial-recognition boarding untouched — but compared with the status quo of unconsented biometric collection by a federal agency, the bill would be a clear net gain for travelers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with bipartisan support in May 2025 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or any further action; Congress is still in session, so it is not yet dead.

narrative.text: Senator Jeff Merkley introduced the Traveler Privacy Protection Act of 2025 on May 8, 2025, joined at introduction by five senators from both parties: Republicans John Kennedy, Roger Marshall, and Steve Daines, and Democrats Ed Markey and Chris Van Hollen.

The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, where it has remained with no committee markup, hearing, or floor action in the record since.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: TSA can keep scanning faces at checkpoints under its current rules, and facial recognition vendors keep their federal airport deployments. Travelers have gained nothing yet, though the bipartisan sponsorship keeps the bill technically alive.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: TSA and its biometric vendors, for now

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship crossed party lines — 3 of 55 Senate Republicans and 2 of 45 Senate Democrats signed on — but the bill has drawn no committee or floor action either way.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and biometric security vendors
industries.note: TSA has been deploying face-matching at airport checkpoints, and this bill would make that technology strictly consent-based, cap how long images are kept, bar sharing the data, and require annual bias audits. Vendors would lose a growing federal market if travelers default to photo IDs.

The bill restricts only TSA's use of facial recognition at screening, leaving airlines' own facial-recognition boarding and other airport uses untouched. That carve-out preserves the private-sector biometric pathway even as the government's is narrowed.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has bipartisan sponsorship, which gives it a plausible path in committee, but the overwhelming majority of Senate bills referred to committee never reach the floor, and this one has seen no action in months. Its most realistic route to law would be as a provision attached to a larger aviation or homeland security package; on its own, it is likely to expire with the 119th Congress unless the committee acts.
